summary: For 9–10 year-olds learning formal long multiplication (up to 4-digit × 1-digit and 2-digit × 2-digit), anchor the written algorithm in the area model so the two partial-product rows and the placeholder zero become meaningful place-value facts rather than memorised rules. The central objective: the child sees that the second partial-product row is '×20 (tens)', not '×2', and that the four sub-rectangles of an area model sum to the same total as the two added partial products. Estimation by rounding both factors bounds the answer and catches magnitude slips.
misconceptions: Omitting the placeholder zero on the second partial product (treating ×20 as ×2).
Multiplying only by the ones digit of the two-digit multiplier and forgetting the tens.
Carrying errors across several columns, or adding carries into the wrong place.
Misaligning partial products when adding them.
Not connecting the algorithm to the area model, so errors can't be self-diagnosed.

activities.title: Bridge the area model to the written method (34 × 27)
steps: Estimate first by rounding both factors: 34 × 27 ≈ 30 × 30 = 900, and keep this estimate in view as you work.
Draw an area model for 34 × 27 and partition it into four labelled sub-rectangles: 30×20, 30×7, 4×20, 4×7.
Alongside, set up the long-multiplication layout and compute the first partial product 34 × 7 = 238 (which is the 30×7 and 4×7 tiles: 210 + 28).
Compute the second partial product 34 × 20 = 680, writing a 0 in the ones place FIRST because this whole row is ×20, i.e. tens (this is the 30×20 and 4×20 tiles: 600 + 80).
Add the two partial products: 238 + 680 = 918, and confirm it matches the sum of all four area tiles (600 + 210 + 80 + 28 = 918).
Check the result against your estimate of 900 — are they close?
activities.insight: The second partial-product row is shifted and carries a placeholder zero because it is ×20 (tens), not ×2; the four area sub-rectangles are exactly the same quantities as the two written partial products broken apart, so the algorithm and the area model are two views of the same calculation.

activities.title: Secure 4-digit × 1-digit short multiplication (2,347 × 6)
steps: Estimate first: 2,347 × 6 ≈ 2,000 × 6 = 12,000 (or 2,300 × 6 = 13,800 for a tighter bound).
Compute 2,347 × 6 in formal written layout, carrying across each column: 7×6=42 (write 2 carry 4), 4×6=24 plus 4 = 28 (write 8 carry 2), 3×6=18 plus 2 = 20 (write 0 carry 2), 2×6=12 plus 2 = 14.
Read off the answer 14,082 and check it against your estimate.
activities.insight: Multiplying a multi-digit number by a single digit requires multiplying every digit and correctly handling carries across several columns; estimation bounds the magnitude.

activities.title: Map each written partial product to its area region (45 × 23)
steps: Draw an area model for 45 × 23 with four regions: 40×20, 40×3, 5×20, 5×3.
Add all four regions to get the product: 800 + 120 + 100 + 15 = 1,035.
Now compute 45 × 23 by long multiplication and point to which area regions make up each partial product: 45×3 = 135 (= 120 + 15) and 45×20 = 900 (= 800 + 100).
Confirm the two partial products 135 + 900 = 1,035 equal the sum of the four area regions.
activities.insight: Each written partial product is a sum of two area sub-rectangles, so a child who can map regions to partials understands WHY there are two rows rather than following steps by rote.

activities.title: Consolidation: spot-the-error and estimate checks
steps: Examine a worked 34 × 27 in which the placeholder zero is missing from the second partial product; identify the error and explain why the zero belongs there.
Fill in a missing second partial product in a given long-multiplication layout.
Choose or state the best estimate for 48 × 52 by rounding both factors (≈ 50 × 50 = 2,500).
activities.insight: The missing placeholder zero and estimation are the quickest self-checks for magnitude; recognising the error reinforces the place-value reasoning behind the shifted row.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to compute 34 × 27 by long multiplication while you watch, and separately to compute 2,347 × 6. Then ask them to draw an area (grid) model for 45 × 23 and point to where each partial product sits. Watch the placeholder zero on the tens row and whether the partial products match the area regions.
checkAnswer: 34 × 27 = 918 (34×7 = 238, 34×20 = 680, sum 918). 2,347 × 6 = 14,082. Area model for 45×23 has four regions 40×20=800, 40×3=120, 5×20=100, 5×3=15, sum 1035. The teacher watches for the placeholder zero when multiplying by the tens digit, correct partial products, and the child mapping each grid region to a partial product.
